Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Morocco's national HMIS development (WB ~2017) notes fragmented systems with paper-based data collection at service delivery level, including rural primary facilities like clinics and dispensaries, with aggregate entry higher up. WHO EMRO eHealth profile indicates no national EHR, N/A EHR usage in primary care facilities (clinics/health centers). Recent EHR in urban hospitals (e.g., HOSIX since 2009, BMC 2025 study), slow expansion to primary/secondary (120M USD plan), pilots like digital prescriptions (2026). No evidence of facility-level digital patient records/registers in rural clinics; HMIS likely aggregate reporting. Digitalisation predominantly paper at rural clinics with emerging pilots/digital aggregate systems.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) rested on an old (~2015) WHO eHealth country profile survey, a World Bank HMIS report link that now returns a DSpace login wall (dead link), and a PMC article blocked by a bot-check on fetch (could not be verified directly). Fresh search finds a World Bank Health Sector Support PforR document confirming the national digitised health information system (SMIPF-SC, covering MNCH/family planning/curative care) was operationalised in 100% of public health centres across all regions by c.2019-2022, with facility-level data captured digitally then aggregated upward. A 2026-published qualitative field study (fieldwork Sept 2024-Mar 2025) in the peripheral Guelmim-Oued Noun region, covering a rural health centre among its three case sites, found the Dossier Medical Informatise (DMI)/BILMED system in active use, improving coordination but constrained by poor connectivity and staff resistance - a genuine but incomplete shift from paper. This is stronger and more current evidence than the original sources and supports moving the score from Entirely paper to Mostly paper - some digital rather than confirming full paper reliance.
revised_comments: Morocco's rural primary healthcare clinics increasingly use digital systems for data capture alongside paper. The national health information system (SMIPF-SC) has been rolled out to all public health centres for maternal, child health, family planning and curative care data, and primary care facilities in peripheral regions use electronic medical record tools (DMI/BILMED). A 2024-2025 field study of a rural health centre in Guelmim-Oued Noun found these digital tools improving care coordination but still constrained by unreliable connectivity, insufficient maintenance and staff adaptation challenges, meaning paper remains in routine use alongside digital records.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Morocco (1282 principal rural offices out of ~2200 total) primarily use paper-based handwritten ledgers for birth registration, with no connected computer systems in the majority as of 2018 World Bank ID4D Diagnostic. Citizens obtain certified paper copies from local offices. Aggregate data is reported upward manually. In 2025, a national project (194M MAD) launched to digitize 38M historical records across all 1821 offices, including rural via regional lots (e.g., southern rural regions), involving manual entry of paper records and connecting offices to a unified system Morocco World News. Law 36.21 (2023) enables e-pre-declarations, but point-of-service recording remains paper-default. No evidence majority rural facilities use digital at point of care; project indicates ongoing transition from paper. Barriers: poor rural IT infrastructure, decentralization. National ambition (Digital Morocco 2030) outpaces rural reality, with digitization as upward reporting/pilot-like effort.

revision_notes: The original score of 1 (Entirely paper) relied on a 2018 World Bank ID4D diagnostic and 2025 press coverage of the historical-records digitisation tender, both of which describe the archival backlog rather than current point-of-registration practice. A more directly relevant source - an October 2024 report citing the Ministry of Interior - states that the Systeme de Gestion de l'Etat Civil (SGEC) is 'generalise sur l'ensemble des bureaux de l'etat civil du Royaume' (deployed nationwide across all civil registry offices) and had processed over 1.3 million birth/death/marriage-related acts through the digital system, covering declaration of births, deaths, marginal notes and marriage/divorce mentions. This indicates that data capture at the point of registration - not just aggregate reporting - is now predominantly digital nationwide, including in rural offices, even though a very large historical paper archive (up to 55 million records dating to 1915) is still being digitised and physical registers/tomes continue to be maintained in parallel per programme documentation. This justifies raising the score from Entirely paper to Mostly digital - some paper.
revised_comments: Morocco's civil registry offices, including those in rural areas, capture vital events primarily through the Systeme de Gestion de l'Etat Civil (SGEC), a digital case-management system for birth, death, marriage and divorce declarations that the Ministry of Interior describes as deployed across the entirety of the Kingdom's civil registry offices. As of late 2024 the system had processed over 1.3 million acts. A parallel Ministry of Interior programme is digitising a historical paper archive of tens of millions of records dating to 1915, and legally-mandated physical registers continue to be maintained alongside the digital system, so some paper-based elements remain in routine use.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Morocco's police (DGSN) and gendarmerie are digitizing case management. DGSN's GESTARR system with integrated crime/delinquency management and procedure digitization is deployed in urban prefectures, regional sûretés (e.g., rural Ouarzazate, Errachidia, Taza), and provincial sûretés, with national rollout planned Mafrique, AllAfrica. Royal Gendarmerie uses HID Livescan for digital biometric booking, replacing outdated manual processes, usable at remote outposts YouTube. Justice sector advancing with online criminal records Justice.gov.ma. No evidence of entirely digital initial recording at all rural stations; ongoing pilots/rollout in some rural areas indicates predominant paper with growing digital systems (score 2). No mentions of paper-only in recent sources; HR reports lack specifics on recording methods.

revision_notes: Reviewed original sources: the DGSN 2024 bilan (GESTARR case-management system, mafrique.ma) is confirmed current; the AllAfrica mirror could not be fetched (crawl timeout) but its content duplicates the mafrique.ma original; the online judicial-record portal (casierjudiciaire.justice.gov.ma) is a citizen-facing request service, not evidence of digitisation at the point of case recording, so it does not directly support the score. Fresh search finds that GESTARR's successor case-management system 'Qadaya' covered 16 of 22 surete (police) commandements as of December 2025, and that digitisation of traffic-accident reports is now complete across all DGSN commandements. However, DGSN's remit is largely urban and semi-urban; genuinely rural policing in Morocco falls mainly to the Gendarmerie Royale, for which no comparably strong 2024-2025 evidence of facility-level digitisation was found beyond the previously-cited use of mobile biometric booking devices at remote outposts. Given rollout remains partial and the strongest recent evidence concerns urban/regional DGSN commandements rather than rural gendarmerie brigades specifically, the original score of Mostly paper - some digital is confirmed rather than raised.
revised_comments: Digital case-management systems (GESTARR, and its successor Qadaya) are progressively being rolled out across Moroccan police commandements, reaching 16 of 22 as of December 2025, and digitisation of traffic-accident reports is now complete nationwide within the national police (DGSN). Rural areas, however, are primarily policed by the Gendarmerie Royale, where digitisation is more limited: mobile biometric booking devices are used at some remote outposts, but most case and incident recording in rural gendarmerie brigades continues to rely substantially on paper alongside these emerging digital tools.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Morocco has a national EMIS called "Pathway," as noted in UNESCO UIS EMIS Typology report. MCC projects provide technical assistance to improve EMIS capabilities nationwide, including student assessments (Mathematica MCC project). Recent initiatives like Orange Foundation's "Écoles numériques" equip 55 rural primary schools with digital tools and content, training teachers, but this is a pilot (Medias24). No direct evidence of routine digital recording at rural schools for attendance/enrollment/grades; typical for EMIS in developing countries to involve paper collection at schools with later digital aggregation at higher levels. Recent digital academy and AI programs indicate growing digital infrastructure, but rural primary facilities likely predominantly paper-based with some pilots/projects. Score 2.

revision_notes: The original score of 2 rested on a general UNESCO EMIS typology paper, an MCC/Mathematica project page, and a report on the Orange Foundation's small 'Ecoles numeriques' pilot (55 additional rural schools in 2024, following 16 in prior years) - all describing supplementary equipment/pilots rather than the core national school information system. Fresh search establishes that Massar, the Ministry of Education's national school-management information system deployed since 2013, is mandatory for all public and private schools including primary schools, and is used directly by teachers and administrators for real-time grade entry ('Massar Prof'), absence recording, enrolment/national student ID issuance and transcript management - i.e. digital data capture at the facility rather than later aggregation. A November 2024 news report of technical problems with Massar enrolment specifically in the rural Zagora region confirms that rural primary schools are in fact using the system directly (with connectivity/performance issues) rather than remaining paper-based. Known limitations persist (absence recording is 'declarative' rather than automated, and remote-area connectivity is a documented adoption barrier), consistent with a mostly-digital-some-paper rather than entirely-digital categorisation. This supports raising the score.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Morocco use the Ministry of Education's national school information system, Massar, which has been mandatory nationwide since 2013 for enrolment, national student identification, grade entry and absence recording, with teachers and administrators entering data directly rather than compiling it on paper for later aggregation. Rural schools are demonstrably using the system in practice, as evidenced by 2024 reports of technical difficulties during enrolment in a rural province, though connectivity and infrastructure constraints in remote areas remain an acknowledged barrier, and supplementary paper-based practices and small-scale digital-equipment pilots (e.g. the Orange Foundation's 'Ecoles numeriques' programme) continue alongside the core digital system.
